strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and proposes a useful feed-forward, promptable interface for both interactive and automatic 3D part segmentation.

The combination of a triplane encoder, SAM-style decoder, and large-scale native 3D supervision is practically compelling. The model-in-the-loop pipeline scales training to a reported 500k shapes and over five million parts.
Reported improvements over Point-SAM are large on both evaluation datasets, especially in the one-click setting, and the qualitative results cover varied artist-created and generated assets.

The appendix includes useful encoder and training-data ablations, implementation details, and runtime comparisons; the ablations support the value of both learnable 3D features and expanded supervision.
weaknesses: The central open-world evaluation may suffer from training-test contamination. Training explicitly incorporates Objaverse and PartNet, while evaluation uses PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNetE, but the paper provides no split construction, asset identifiers, deduplication procedure, or statement that evaluation shapes were excluded. Without demonstrated disjointness, the large gains and generalization claims are not reliable.

The headline automatic-segmentation comparison materially changes PartField by disabling its native connectivity-based clustering while leaving other methods in their original settings. Appendix Table 4 shows trained PartField with connectivity reaching 79.2 IoU, above PartSAM's main-table 69.5, whereas PartSAM reaches 81.3 after also using connectivity. Thus, the claimed greater-than-20% improvement depends strongly on an asymmetric comparison; both connectivity-on and connectivity-off results should be reported prominently.

The automatic metric is insufficiently specified and potentially favors methods producing many proposals: performance uses the best IoU among multi-scale candidate masks, without clearly penalizing duplicate, spurious, overlapping, or uncovered regions. Important inference parameters, including the number of prompt samples and predicted-IoU filtering threshold, are also omitted.

The presentation overstates independence from 2D supervision. The encoder is initialized from PartField and retains a frozen branch containing SAM-distilled priors; the ablations indicate these priors materially help. Claims that the method is unlike approaches transferring knowledge from 2D foundation models therefore need qualification.

The model-in-the-loop filtering is circular: PartField pseudo-labels are accepted when the current PartSAM can reproduce them under error-driven prompts. This measures agreement and model compatibility, not semantic correctness, and may reinforce both models' biases. No human audit, annotation precision estimate, or comparison against independently labeled data validates the claimed label quality.

Evidence for the claimed understanding of internal 3D structure is mostly qualitative. There is no dedicated held-out benchmark or quantitative analysis of internal versus visible-surface parts, despite this being a central motivation.

Reproducibility is limited: the code and model are only promised, the complete dataset composition and licensing are unspecified, training/evaluation seeds and uncertainty are absent, and several results differ without explanation between Tables 1-2 and the ablation table (for example, automatic IoU 69.5 versus 68.5). Overall, the idea and reported results are promising, but the unresolved data leakage and evaluation-fairness issues keep the paper below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and presents a practically attractive feed-forward, promptable framework for open-world 3D part segmentation.

The combination of a triplane feature field, dual frozen/trainable encoder branches, and a SAM-style decoder is technically coherent. The model also supports both interactive segmentation and automatic proposal generation.
The reported interactive gains over Point-SAM are substantial on both evaluated benchmarks, particularly for a single prompt.
The component and data ablations provide useful evidence that encoder adaptation and the expanded pseudo-labeled corpus contribute to performance.
The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and includes implementation, computational-cost, and qualitative application details.
weaknesses: The automatic-segmentation comparison is not convincing or fair. The main experiment disables mesh connectivity for PartField even though connectivity is fundamental to that method. Table 4 shows the original pretrained PartField with connectivity reaching 79.2 IoU, substantially above PartSAM's headline 69.5 result. PartSAM only reaches 81.3 after adding its own connectivity-based graph-cut postprocessing, reducing the apparent advantage to 2.1 points. This directly undermines the claimed greater-than-20% improvement over the strongest baseline.

Potential train-test contamination is not addressed. Training assets are mined from Objaverse and PartNet, while evaluation uses PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNetE. The paper gives no asset-level exclusion, deduplication, or split audit demonstrating that benchmark shapes or near duplicates are absent from the 500k-shape training corpus.

The automatic metric appears to select the best candidate mask and best granularity for each ground-truth instance, including an oracle sweep over four NMS thresholds. Such best-match IoU does not penalize false-positive, overlapping, redundant, or uncovered masks and therefore does not establish the claim that the system reliably decomposes an entire shape. Partition-level metrics, proposal precision/recall, coverage, and a fixed validation-selected threshold are needed.

The model-in-the-loop annotation criterion is circular: agreement between PartSAM and a PartField pseudo-label shows that the pseudo-label is reproducible under prompts, not that it is semantically correct. There is no representative human audit, annotation precision estimate, comparison against ground truth, or analysis of systematic pseudo-label bias.

The central positioning as training natively in 3D and avoiding dependence on 2D foundation-model supervision is overstated. Both encoder branches are initialized from PartField, one branch permanently preserves SAM-distilled priors, and much of the added supervision is generated by PartField. The method therefore still depends materially on SAM-derived 2D knowledge.

Experimental breadth is limited. Interactive segmentation is compared only with Point-SAM despite discussion of other interactive systems; the important claims about interior geometry and AI-generated meshes receive only selected qualitative examples; and no cross-dataset, corruption, input-modality, or category-level analysis is provided.

Important reporting details are absent, including benchmark and mask sample counts, uncertainty across runs, complete data-source composition and licenses, exact train/test exclusions, filtering thresholds, and sufficient evaluation-code details. The code and model are only promised for future release, while the newly curated dataset is not clearly committed for release.

The architectural novelty is moderate because the main ingredients largely combine SAM's interaction/decoding design with a PartField-based triplane encoder. Given this incremental construction, especially rigorous and leakage-free evaluation is necessary, but the current evidence does not meet that standard.

strengths: PartSAM addresses an important problem with a useful combination of promptable interaction, feed-forward inference, and automatic multi-granularity decomposition for 3D parts.

The large-scale native-3D data pipeline is a meaningful contribution: the paper expands supervision to roughly 500K shapes and five million parts and provides evidence that the model-in-the-loop annotations improve performance.
Results are strong across two benchmarks. The particularly large single-click gains over Point-SAM and consistent improvements in automatic segmentation indicate practical value.
The dual-branch triplane encoder is well motivated: it preserves pretrained PartField/SAM-derived priors while learning from native 3D labels and incorporating normals and color.
Ablations cover encoder choices and training-data variants, while the complexity analysis shows a favorable approximately 12-second feed-forward runtime compared with optimization-based approaches.
The paper is clearly organized, visually compelling, and includes useful qualitative results on artist-created and AI-generated meshes.
weaknesses: The central open-world generalization claim needs stronger safeguards against data leakage. Training uses Objaverse and PartNet-derived assets while evaluation uses PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNetE, but asset-level overlap checks, deduplication procedures, and category-disjoint splits are not documented.

The main automatic-segmentation comparison modifies PartField by removing mesh connectivity, an essential component of that method, while allowing SAMesh to retain connectivity. The appendix shows standard connectivity substantially improves PartField, making the claimed margin over prior work less decisive than Table 2 suggests.

The automatic metric appears to oracle-match each ground-truth part to the best candidate across several granularities. This does not penalize duplicate, spurious, or incomplete decompositions; matching-based metrics, precision/recall, or segmentation covering measures would provide a more faithful evaluation.

The model-in-the-loop annotations are accepted using agreement between PartField pseudo-labels and PartSAM interactions rather than independent semantic validation. A human-audited sample with precision estimates and comparisons against simpler filtering strategies is needed.

The claimed advantage for interior geometry is supported primarily by selected qualitative examples. A quantitative evaluation on occluded or internal parts would be important because this is a central motivation for native-3D supervision.
The method remains dependent on PartField weights containing SAM-derived 2D priors, so descriptions implying independence from transferred 2D foundation-model knowledge are overstated.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the full composition and licensing of the training corpus, train/test exclusion rules, several automatic-mode details, variance across runs, and released artifacts are not yet provided. Small unexplained discrepancies also appear between the main and ablation results.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: controllable, open-world 3D part segmentation with feed-forward inference and support for internal or occluded geometry.

PartSAM combines a prompt-guided decoder with a scalable triplane encoder in a technically sensible design. The frozen/learnable dual-branch construction is well motivated and the main architectural alternatives are ablated.
The proposed data-curation effort is substantial, scaling supervision to approximately 500K shapes and five million parts. The model-in-the-loop pipeline is an interesting practical contribution.

Reported improvements are large on both interactive and automatic segmentation, and the paper includes results on multiple benchmarks, scaling experiments, runtime analysis, qualitative examples, applications, and failure cases.
The presentation is generally clear and visually strong, and the appendix provides useful architecture and training details.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not establish that benchmark objects were excluded from training. Training uses Objaverse/Objaverse-XL and PartNet, while evaluation uses PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNetE. Without explicit ID-level deduplication and split information, direct or near-duplicate leakage is a serious possibility that undermines the central open-world generalization claim.

The automatic-segmentation metric appears oracle-like: multiple segmentations or candidate masks are generated across NMS thresholds, and the best IoU against ground truth is reported. The protocol is insufficiently specified and seemingly does not penalize false-positive parts, redundant proposals, or incoherent whole-object decompositions. Standard partition or proposal metrics and a fixed operating point are needed.

The headline PartObjaverse comparison modifies PartField by disabling mesh connectivity, even though connectivity is integral to that method. Under the common connectivity-enabled setting reported in the appendix, PartField reaches 79.2 IoU and PartSAM 81.3, far smaller than the main-table gap of 69.5 versus 51.5. Both common-setting comparisons should be prominent, and claims of large superiority should be qualified.

The claimed native-3D distinction is overstated. PartSAM initializes both branches from PartField, preserves a frozen branch containing SAM-derived 2D priors, and obtains much of its second-stage supervision from PartField pseudo-labels. The experiments do not isolate native labels from these inherited 2D priors sufficiently to support several broad causal claims.

Pseudo-label quality is not validated by independent human annotation. Agreement between PartSAM and PartField measures reproducibility, not semantic correctness, and can preferentially select existing model biases. The assertion that residual errors are negligible is unsupported; scaling-curve improvement does not establish annotation precision.

Interactive evaluation compares primarily against Point-SAM, omitting other relevant interactive systems and providing no uncertainty estimates. The retrained Point-SAM result in the appendix also differs substantially from the main-table baseline, making the main comparison less informative about architecture versus training-data scale.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the exact source datasets and licenses, source-specific counts, benchmark-overlap filtering, several curation thresholds, predicted-IoU rejection threshold, final mask threshold, automatic evaluation/matching procedure, and release plans for code, models, and curated annotations are not specified. There is also an inconsistency between the stated RGB/normal inputs and the appendix description of additional channels.

Because possible training-test contamination and the oracle/fairness issues affect the main quantitative evidence, the otherwise promising technical contribution is not currently supported strongly enough for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: promptable, open-world 3D part segmentation with fast feed-forward inference.
The SAM-style interaction mechanism combined with a triplane encoder is practically useful, and the reported one-click results substantially exceed Point-SAM.
The scale of the curated training corpus—approximately 500K shapes and five million shape-part pairs—is potentially valuable.
The paper includes architecture and data ablations, scaling results, runtime comparisons, evaluation on several benchmarks, qualitative examples, and an explicit discussion of failure cases.
The presentation is generally clear, and the automatic and interactive operating modes are well motivated.
weaknesses: The principal automatic-segmentation comparison is not fair. The authors disable mesh connectivity for PartField even though it is integral to that method, while retaining connectivity for SAMesh. Table 4 shows that standard PartField with connectivity scores 79.2, substantially above PartSAM's headline 69.5 without connectivity; PartSAM only reaches 81.3 after receiving similar connectivity-based post-processing. This undermines the claimed large margin over the state of the art.

A potentially serious train-test contamination issue is left unresolved. Training data are mined from Objaverse/Objaverse-XL, while the main benchmark is PartObjaverse-Tiny, yet the paper provides no object-ID deduplication procedure or explicit confirmation that evaluation assets were excluded from training and pseudo-label generation.

The claim of native 3D semantic supervision is overstated. Much of the supervision comes from scene-graph nodes, connected components, or PartField pseudo-labels; PartField itself inherits SAM-derived 2D knowledge, as does the frozen encoder branch. These signals need not correspond to semantic parts.

The model-in-the-loop filter is circular: pseudo-labels are retained when PartSAM can reproduce them using prompts and error regions derived from those same labels. This measures agreement and ease of interactive fitting, not semantic correctness. No human audit, annotation precision estimate, or comparison against independently labeled data is provided, while the assertion that residual errors are negligible is unsupported.

Interactive evaluation uses idealized central first clicks and subsequent clicks selected with access to ground-truth error regions. There is no evaluation with realistic, noisy, boundary-adjacent, or human-generated prompts, despite controllability being a central claim.

Interactive comparisons are limited mainly to Point-SAM. Relevant interactive systems such as iSeg are discussed but not evaluated. Moreover, the headline comparison contrasts PartSAM's much larger native-data training regime against the released Point-SAM; the same-data retraining appears only as an appendix ablation, leaving data and architecture gains insufficiently disentangled.

The quantitative automatic-segmentation protocol is under-specified and partly oracle-driven: results select the best candidate across scales or NMS thresholds, but the precise instance matching, aggregation, threshold-selection policy, and treatment of overlapping or uncovered regions are not adequately defined.

Claims about AI-generated meshes and interior structures rely almost entirely on selected qualitative examples. There is no annotated quantitative benchmark isolating interior, occluded, disconnected, or generated geometry, so the key claimed advantage over 2D-lifted methods is not convincingly established.

Reproducibility is limited: the exact training asset list and licenses, deduplication rules, pseudo-label corpus, preprocessing details, and release commitment are missing. The blank project-page entry compounds this concern. The paper also does not adequately discuss licensing implications of mining large online asset collections.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence—for example, attributing gains to avoidance of catastrophic forgetting without measuring forgetting, calling automatic decomposition an emergent capability despite a substantial engineered proposal-and-NMS pipeline, and describing the work as a foundation model based on relatively narrow evaluation.

Overall, the method is promising, but the baseline manipulation, possible benchmark overlap, circular data validation, and insufficient evidence for the central native-3D claims are major issues rather than minor omissions. These prevent the submission from meeting the acceptance bar.

strengths: The paper makes a clear, relevant contribution: a feed-forward, promptable 3D part-segmentation system trained with millions of native 3D shape-part pairs, addressing controllability and interior-geometry limitations of predominantly 2D-lifting or clustering-based approaches.

The empirical gains are large and consistent. PartSAM substantially improves one-click interactive IoU over Point-SAM on PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNet-E, and outperforms several strong methods on automatic segmentation across both benchmarks.

The evaluation covers interactive and automatic segmentation, generated meshes, interior and occluded structures, real-world scans, and the independent 3DCoMPaT++ benchmark. The qualitative results are extensive and include randomly sampled outputs and explicit failure cases.

The ablations support the principal design choices: pretrained initialization, the frozen/learnable dual-branch encoder, large-scale data, and model-in-the-loop annotations all yield measurable benefits. The scaling curve further shows continued improvement up to 500K shapes.

The method is practically attractive: inference is feed-forward, much faster than optimization-based lifting approaches, supports adjustable granularity, and provides interactive refinement and automatic decomposition in one framework.
The manuscript is well organized, visually clear, and unusually candid about limitations such as rare surface details, ambiguous part hierarchies, and the absence of semantic labels.
weaknesses: Potential train-test contamination is not adequately addressed. The training corpus is mined from Objaverse/Objaverse-XL while PartObjaverse-Tiny is also derived from Objaverse, but the paper does not document asset-level deduplication or similarity filtering. This is especially important given the strong connectivity-derived supervision available in artist-created meshes.

The quality of the model-in-the-loop annotations is insufficiently validated. Pseudo-labels originate from PartField and are accepted according to agreement with PartSAM, creating possible confirmation bias; a statistically meaningful human audit of semantic validity, boundary quality, and retained/rejected-label precision is missing.

The paper overstates the distinction from 2D-derived approaches. Although the supervision added by the authors is native 3D, both encoder branches are initialized from PartField, whose representations distill SAM priors, and one branch remains frozen. Thus the final model still materially depends on transferred 2D knowledge.

Interactive evaluation compares only against Point-SAM. Comparisons with other interactive or prompt-adaptable 3D methods, and controlled baselines using the same encoder or training data, would better isolate the benefit of the proposed decoder and training procedure.

Automatic segmentation uses an oracle-style best score over several granularities or candidate masks. While this follows a prior protocol, it does not fully measure how well a deployable method selects granularity without ground truth. Results for a fixed, validation-selected operating point and metrics penalizing over/under-segmentation would strengthen the claims.

Important evaluation details are underspecified, including test-set sample counts, uncertainty across runs, exact mask-matching/aggregation procedures, and robustness to prompt placement. The reported improvements are large, but error bars and random-prompt evaluations are still needed.

Reproducibility and data governance remain incomplete: there is no explicit release commitment, the complete dataset composition and filtering thresholds are not fully specified, and licensing/deduplication procedures for the large collection of online assets require clearer documentation.
